ety.text: From Middle English from (“from”), from Old English from, fram (“forward, from”), from Proto-West Germanic *fram, from Proto-Germanic *fram (“forward, from, away”). Cognate with Old Saxon fram (“from”) and Old High German fram (“from”), Danish frem (“forth, forward”), Danish fra (“from”), Swedish fram (“forth, forward”), Swedish från (“from”), Norwegian Nynorsk fram (“forward”), Norwegian Nynorsk frå (“from”), Icelandic fram (“forward, on”), Icelandic frá (“from”), Albanian pre, prej. More at fro.

senses.d: With reference to the location or position of a speaker or other observer or vantage point.

From Middle English front, frunt, frount, from Old French front, frunt, from Latin frōns, frontem (“forehead”). Doublet of frons.

senses.d: The foremost side of something or the end that faces the direction it normally moves.
The side of a building with the main entrance.
ex: I'll go out the front, and you go out the back.

senses.d: A field of activity.
A person or institution acting as the public face of some other, covert group.
ex: Near-synonyms: frontperson, frontman, front man

senses.d: The interface or transition zone between two airmasses of different density, often resulting in precipitation. Since the temperature distribution is the most important regulator of atmospheric density, a front almost invariably separates airmasses of different temperature.
ex: We need to take the clothes off the line. The news reported a front is coming in from the east, and we can expect heavy rain and maybe hail.

senses.d: An area where armies are engaged in conflict, especially the line of contact.

A major military subdivision of the Soviet Army.
Located at or near the front.
ex: The front runner was thirty meters ahead of her nearest competitor.

senses.d: Pronounced with the highest part of the body of the tongue toward the front of the mouth, near the hard palate (most often describing a vowel).
ex: The English word dress has a front vowel in most dialects.

senses.d: Closest or nearest, of a set of futures contracts which expire at particular times, or of the times they expire; (typically, the front month or front year is the next calendar month or year after the current one).
ex: Contracts are available for every month in the front year but do not extend over a year.

senses.d: To face (on, to); to be pointed in a given direction.
ex: The palazzo has always fronted on a bus stop—but this putative man of the people has kindly put an end to that public service.
The great gate fronting to the north was about four feet high, and almost two feet wide, through which I could easily creep.

senses.d: To face, be opposite to.
ex: She sat on a seat under the alders in the cricket ground, and fronted the evening.

senses.d: To face up to, to meet head-on, to confront.
ex:
Know you not Gaueston hath store of golde,
Which may in Ireland purchase him such friends,
As he will front the mightiest of vs all,

senses.d: To adorn with, at the front; to put on the front.

senses.d: To pronounce with the tongue in a front position.

senses.d: To move (a word or clause) to the start of a sentence (or series of adjectives, etc).
